Stage 3 · Reading

The house that talks to itself

Fourteen connected devices in an average home, and the one night in 2016 that showed what they add up to.

🏠📶
1 · Before you read. Which of these worries you most about a smart device in your home?

Choose one and say why. Compare with a partner before you read.Choose one and say why before you read.Choose one and note your reason. You will check it against the text.

The house that talks to itself

Written for this course, from reporting on the October 2016 attack on Dyn and from the UK Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022, enforced from April 2024.

1The phrase “internet of things” describes something very ordinary: objects which contain a small computer and a wireless connection. A smoke detector that tells you which room is on fire is one. So is a smart meter, which reports your electricity use without anybody reading a dial. None of this is new technology. What changed was the price, and a house with high-speed broadband now carries around fourteen internet-connected devices, most of which its owners could not list.

2The technical problems that worried engineers in the 1990s were solved years ago. The ones that matter now are about who can access what, and the clearest demonstration came on 21 October 2016. Users across the United States found that Twitter, Netflix and Reddit had become unreachable, for hours. The cause was not a hostile government. It was a flood of traffic aimed at Dyn, a company which ran part of the internet’s address system, and the flood was produced by ordinary household objects.

3The software behind it, which was named Mirai after a cartoon, was not sophisticated. It simply worked through a short list of about sixty usernames and passwords — the ones that cameras, routers and recorders are sold with — and tried them on every device it could find. A camera that can be hacked from the street is worse than no camera at all, and hundreds of thousands of machines whose owners had never changed a password were quietly recruited. Anyone whose baby monitor took part in that attack is still unaware of it. The code was published online, and variants of it are still responsible for a measurable share of attacks today.

4Governments have been slow, and then sudden. In April 2024 the United Kingdom became the first country to ban universal default passwords on consumer devices that connect to the internet. The law, which covers everything from doorbells to fridges, also requires manufacturers to publish a contact point for anybody who finds a fault, and it carries fines of up to ten million pounds. It is a small rule that addresses a large share of the problem, which tells you how basic the problem was.

5The interesting risk, though, is duller than a botnet. The data any single device sends is trivial: a kettle boiled at 6.40, a light switched off at 23.10, a doorbell that nobody answered on Thursday. Put together, those readings describe a life — when the house is empty, who sleeps badly, whether anybody is ill. That pattern, which nobody ever agreed to hand over, is what the argument about privacy is actually about, and no password will fix it.

6Which may explain a small oddity. The users who are most tech-savvy, who understand exactly how little each individual reading contains, are often the ones with the fewest smart devices installed at home. They are not worried about being watched. They are worried about being described. Everybody else is told that the technology is convenient, which it is, and left to discover the rest.

Text A · The night the sites went dark

Written for this course, from reporting on the October 2016 attack on Dyn and the UK Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act 2022.

Users across the United States found that Twitter, Netflix and Reddit had become unreachable, for hours. The cause was not a hostile government. It was a flood of traffic aimed at Dyn, a company which ran part of the internet’s address system, and the flood was produced by ordinary household objects.

The software behind it, which was named Mirai after a cartoon, was not sophisticated. It simply worked through a short list of about sixty usernames and passwords — the ones that cameras, routers and recorders are sold with — and tried them on every device it could find. Text B · The risk that no password fixes

Written for this course.

Governments have been slow, and then sudden. In April 2024 the United Kingdom became the first country to ban universal default passwords on consumer devices that connect to the internet. The law, which covers everything from doorbells to fridges, also requires manufacturers to publish a contact point for anybody who finds a fault, and it carries fines of up to ten million pounds. It is a small rule that addresses a large share of the problem, which tells you how basic the problem was. Manufacturers had known about the weakness for years and almost none of them had acted, because a device that is cheap to make and quick to install sells better than one that is difficult to break into.

The users who are most tech-savvy, who understand exactly how little each individual reading contains, are often the ones with the fewest smart devices installed at home. They are not worried about being watched. They are worried about being described. Everybody else is told that the technology is convenient, which it is, and left to discover the rest — usually years later, and usually from somebody who is trying to sell them something.

1 · Read the explanation.
Defining and non-defining relative clauses

Two jobs. A defining clause tells you which one is meant: the device that sends the data. Remove it and the sentence no longer identifies anything. A non-defining clause adds information about something already identified: the smart meter, which reports your electricity use, was fitted in March. Remove it and the sentence still works.

Commas and pronouns. Defining clauses take no commas and may use that, which, who. Non-defining clauses take commas and never that. This one rule catches most of the errors at this level.

Leaving the pronoun out. In a defining clause, if the relative pronoun is the object, you can drop it: the password (that) they were sold with, the engineer (who) we called. If it is the subject, it must stay: the device that sends the data, never the device sends the data.

Prepositions. Everyday English puts the preposition at the end: the room that the sensor is in. Formal writing moves it forward, and then that becomes impossible: the room in which the sensor sits.

Whose, where, when. Whose shows possession, for people and things alike: a company whose servers are abroad. Where, when and why follow place, time and reason.

Two special patterns. Quantities take of which or of whom: fourteen devices, most of which…, ten engineers, none of whom…. And a non-defining which can refer to a whole clause: The doorbell has been updated once, which is the problem.

The commonest errors at this level
  • That after a comma: the meter, that reports…
  • Dropping a subject pronoun: the device sends the data is cheap.
  • Keeping the old pronoun as well: the device that it sends the data.
  • Who’s for whose: a company who’s servers are abroad.
  • Commas that change the claim: The engineers, who were tech-savvy, refused says all of them did.

1 — The commas are not decoration. The engineers who were tech-savvy refused says some of them refused. The engineers, who were tech-savvy, refused says all of them did, and adds that they were all tech-savvy. Same words, different fact.

5 · Worked example. Read it before you do the exercises.
Joining two sentences with a relative clause

Start: We replaced the camera. The camera could be hacked from the street.

Step 1 — ask whether the reader already knows which one. Here there were several cameras and this one is being picked out, so the clause is defining: no commas.

Step 2 — choose the pronoun. A thing, and defining, so that or which. Take that.

Step 3 — ask whether it is subject or object in the new clause. The camera does the hacking? No: the camera could be hacked — it is the subject of that clause, so the pronoun must stay.

Step 4 — put it straight after the noun. We replaced the camera that could be hacked from the street.

Now the other version. If there is only one camera and you are adding a fact, it becomes non-defining: We replaced the camera, which could be hacked from the street. Commas, and never that.

13 · Read this before the extra practice.
Two kinds, and the comma that tells them apart

A defining clause says which one I mean. It carries no commas, and without it the sentence does not identify anything: the device that sends the data · the people who installed it. A non-defining clause adds information about something already identified, and sits inside commas: the meter, which reports your use, is new · my neighbour, who is an engineer, refused.

Two consequences follow, and they are the whole lesson. That is impossible in a non-defining clause: the meter, that reports your use, is new. And the pronoun can be dropped only when it is the object of the defining clause: the password (that) they were sold with — but not when it is the subject: the sensor that reports the temperature, where nothing can go.

Read what the comma does to the claim. The devices that were sold before 2018 have no password says only some of them do. The devices, which were sold before 2018, have no password says all of them were sold then, and none of them has a password. One comma, two different worlds.

whose, where, when, and prepositions

whose works for people and things alike: a company whose servers are abroad. where, when and why cover place, time and reason (the hallway where the sensor sits, the year when broadband arrived, the reason why it was never updated) and can be defining or non-defining.

Prepositions have two positions. Everyday English leaves them at the end: the room that the router is in. Formal writing puts them in front, and then that becomes impossible: the room in which the router sits. The same applies to quantity phrases, which are always non-defining: fourteen devices, most of which were still on the default password.

Finally, which can refer to a whole clause rather than a noun, always after a comma: It is convenient, which it certainly is. This is common in speech and in argument, and it is one of the few places where which has no noun in front of it.

Errors to watch: the meter, that reports your use → which · the sensor reports the temperature is broken → the subject pronoun cannot be dropped · the room in that the router sits → in which · a company which servers are abroad → whose.

1 · Read the model guide.
Model · a guide in four paragraphs

A smart doorbell is a device that replaces the button beside your door with a camera, a microphone and a wireless connection. When somebody presses it, or simply walks past, the doorbell sends a short recording to a company’s servers, from which your smartphone collects it a second later. The technology, which is at least fifteen years old, only became ordinary when the price fell below the price of a good lock.

What it collects is more than the visitor. A doorbell facing the street records the people who live opposite, the delivery drivers who come daily and anybody who stops to answer a phone call. Most systems keep those clips for thirty days, which is long enough to show who was where, and when.

Who can access them is the question worth asking in the shop. The answer is normally you, the company whose servers hold the clips, anybody you have shared the app with, and, in some countries, the police on request. Add to that anybody who can hack an account that still uses the password it was sold with.

Two checks, in this order. First, ask what the doorbell does when the broadband fails: a device that stops ringing is worse than the button it replaced. Second, ask how long the clips are kept and whether that can be changed, because the setting you cannot alter is the one that will matter.
